question: Let $A B C$ be an acute triangle. Let $D, E$, and $F$ be the feet of altitudes from $A, B$, and $C$ to sides $\overline{B C}$, $\overline{C A}$, and $\overline{A B}$, respectively, and let $Q$ be the foot of altitude from $A$ to line $E F$. Given that $A Q=20$, $B C=15$, and $A D=24$, compute the perimeter of triangle $D E F$.

completions.text:
We will show that if an acute‐angled triangle ABC has altitudes AD, BE, and CF (with D on BC, etc.) and if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF, then in fact

  EF = (BC)·cos A      (1)

and one may prove that the other two sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF satisfy

  FD = (AB)·cos C  and  DE = (AC)·cos B.

A standard (and very useful) fact is that in any triangle

  (AB)·cos C + (AC)·cos B = BC.    (2)

Then the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = (BC)·cos A + [(AB)·cos C + (AC)·cos B] = (BC)·cos A + BC
                   = BC·(1 + cos A).   (3)

In our problem the given data are:
  BC = 15, AD = 24, and AQ = 20,
where AD is the altitude from A to BC and AQ is the distance from A to EF.

A key (and not hard‐to‐prove) fact is that in an acute triangle the distance from A to EF equals the altitude AD multiplied by cos A. (One way to see this is to show that the line EF is “antiparallel” to BC; then an easy trigonometric argument shows that the distance from A to EF is AD·cos A.) In other words,
  AQ = AD·cos A.
Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24 we deduce that
  cos A = 20/24 = 5/6.

Now using (3) we have
  Perimeter of DEF = BC·(1 + cos A) = 15·(1 + 5/6) = 15·(11/6) = 165/6 = 55/2.

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55/2.

A brief outline of the solution steps is as follows:
1. Recognize that in an acute triangle the feet of the altitudes (the orthic triangle) has sides
  EF = BC·cos A, FD = AB·cos C, DE = AC·cos B.
2. Use the well‐known identity AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
3. Conclude that the perimeter of DEF is BC(1 + cos A).
4. Notice that the distance from A to EF (namely AQ) equals AD·cos A.
5. Substitute the given values AQ = 20 and AD = 24 to find cos A = 20/24 = 5/6.
6. Finally, compute the perimeter: 15·(1 + 5/6) = 55/2.

Therefore, the answer is 55/2.

  E = foot of the B–altitude on CA,

  EF + FD + DE = (BC·cos A) + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(1+cos A).

Now substitute cos A = 4⁄5 into (1):
  Perimeter(DEF) = 15·(1 + 4⁄5) = 15·(9⁄5) = 27.

Therefore, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 27.

We will show that if ABC is an acute‐angled triangle with

  • BC = a = 15,
  • the A–altitude has length AD = 24, and 
  • if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to the side EF of the “orthic triangle” DEF (where D, E, F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C, respectively) and AQ = 20,

then one may prove that

  EF = a·cos A  and  (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = a.

In other words, one may show that the three sides of the orthic triangle are

  EF = a·cos A,
  FD = AC·cos B,
  DE = AB·cos C.

Then its perimeter is

  EF + FD + DE = a·cos A + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = a·cos A + a.

In our problem a = 15 and we will now explain how to “read off” cos A from the data.

Step 1. Relate AQ, AD, and angle A.

A key fact (which you may verify in the special case of an equilateral triangle) is that in any acute triangle the distance from a vertex to the line joining the feet of the other two altitudes equals the length of the altitude from that vertex times cos of the vertex’s angle. (There are several proofs of this fact; one may use similar triangles or vector methods.) In our situation the vertex is A, the altitude from A is AD = 24, and the distance from A to line EF is AQ = 20. Hence

  AQ = AD · cos A  ⟹  cos A = AQ/AD = 20/24 = 5/6.

Step 2. Use a well‐known relation in any triangle.

It is a standard fact that in any triangle with sides a, b, c (with a opposite A, etc.) one has

  b·cos C + c·cos B = a.

(To see this, drop the altitude from A onto BC; then the projections of AB and AC onto BC add to BC.)

Step 3. Write the perimeter of the orthic triangle.

As noted above one may show that the sides of the orthic triangle are
  EF = a·cos A  ,  FD = AC·cos B  ,  DE = AB·cos C.
Thus the perimeter P is

  P = EF + FD + DE 
    = a·cos A + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B)
    = a·cos A + a         [by the relation above]
    = a (cos A + 1).

Now substitute a = 15 and cos A = 5/6:

  P = 15 · (5/6 + 1) = 15 · (5/6 + 6/6) = 15 · (11/6) = (15×11)/6 = 165/6 = 55/2.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55/2.

Final Answer: 55/2.

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15(1 + cos A)        (1)

and then use the fact that in an acute triangle the distance from A to the “side‐EF” of the orthic triangle equals the altitude from A times cos A. (In other words, if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF then

  AQ = AD·cos A.)

In our problem AD = 24 and AQ = 20 so that

  24·cos A = 20  ⟹  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Then (1) gives

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

The remainder of this article explains one way to arrive at (1) and the “key‐fact” about AQ.

────────────────────────────
A little background

Suppose ABC is an acute triangle and let D, E, F be the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C respectively (so that DEF is the “orthic triangle”). A well–known fact is that the side of the orthic triangle opposite A (namely, EF) has length
  EF = BC·cos A.
Similarly one may show that
  FD = AC·cos B  and  DE = AB·cos C.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is
  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + AC·cos B + AB·cos C.
Now, if one expresses AC and AB in terms of the altitude from A (recall that in triangle ABC the altitude from A is AD = 24 and also AD = AC·sin B = AB·sin C) one may show that
  AC·cos B + AB·cos C = 24 (cot B + cot C).
But using the sine–area formula for ΔABC (Area = ½·AB·AC·sin A = 180) one may prove that
  cot B + cot C = 5⁄8.
Since we are given BC = 15 the perimeter becomes
  15 cos A + 24·(5⁄8) = 15 cos A + 15 = 15(1 + cos A).

────────────────────────────
The “key–fact”

One may show (by an easy similarity argument or by using properties of the Simson line) that in an acute triangle the distance from A to the line EF is exactly the altitude from A times cos A; that is,
  AQ = AD·cos A.
(To check this in the special case of an equilateral triangle is a good exercise.) In our problem AQ = 20 and AD = 24 so that
  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.
Then the perimeter of DEF is
  15(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 55⁄2.

────────────────────────────
Answer

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

An answer in boxed form:

  Perimeter(DEF) = 55⁄2.

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF is

  Perimeter = 8√11.

In what follows we describe one solution (there are several) that leads to this answer.

Below is one way to “unlock” the problem.

──────────────────────────────
A. The Setup and Some Known Facts

Suppose triangle ABC is acute with feet of the altitudes
  D on BC, E on CA, F on AB.
Also, let Q be the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF and assume
  AQ = 20, AD = 24, and BC = 15.
A well‐known fact is that the three points D, E, F form what is called the “orthic triangle” of ABC. Moreover, it is known that the nine–point circle of ABC is exactly the circumcircle of DEF and that its radius is R/2 where R is the circumradius of ABC.

There is also a classical fact (which you may verify in the equilateral case) that in an acute triangle the distance from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side of the orthic triangle equals the corresponding altitude times the cosine of that vertex’s angle. (In other words, one may show that)
  AQ = AD·cos A.
Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.
Then
  sin A = √(1 – (5⁄6)²) = √(1 – 25⁄36) = √(11⁄36) = (√11)⁄6.
Also, since side BC is opposite A we have (by the extended law of sines)
  BC = 2R sin A.
But BC = 15, so

  15 = 2R·(√11⁄6) ⟹ R = 15·6⁄(2√11) = 45⁄√11.
──────────────────────────────
B. Expressing the Perimeter of DEF in Terms of R and the Angles

A standard fact is that if a triangle has circumradius r and angles α, β, γ then its side lengths are
  a = 2r sin α, b = 2r sin β, c = 2r sin γ.
Since the circumcircle of DEF is the nine–point circle of ABC it has radius R/2. (Also one may show that the angles of DEF are 180° – 2A, 180° – 2B, and 180° – 2C.) Hence, for example, the side opposite A (namely, EF) is
  EF = 2·(R⁄2)·sin(180° – 2A) = R sin 2A = 2R sin A cos A.
Likewise,
  FD = 2R sin B cos B  and  DE = 2R sin C cos C.
Thus the perimeter P of DEF is
  P = 2R (sin A cos A + sin B cos B + sin C cos C).
But note that
  sin A cos A + sin B cos B + sin C cos C = ½ (sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C).
A well–known trigonometric identity shows that
  sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.
Therefore,
  P = 2R · [½ · 4 sin A sin B sin C] = 4R sin A sin B sin C.
──────────────────────────────
C. Using the Altitude AD

Now, recall that the altitude from A to BC is
  AD = 2R sin B sin C.
But we are given AD = 24, so
  2R sin B sin C = 24 ⟹ sin B sin C = 12⁄R.
Substitute this into the expression for P:
  P = 4R sin A · (12⁄R) = 48 sin A.
We already found sin A = (√11)⁄6, so
  P = 48 · (√11⁄6) = 8√11.
──────────────────────────────
D. Conclusion

Thus, with the given data the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  8√11.

This is the final answer.

──────────────────────────────
Answer: 8√11

A Note on the “AQ = AD cos A” Fact:
One may show (by, for example, using similar–triangles or by a careful angle–chasing argument) that in an acute triangle the distance from a vertex to the line containing the opposite side of the orthic triangle equals the corresponding altitude times the cosine of that vertex’s angle. (You can check this in the special case of an equilateral triangle.) This fact was used above to deduce cos A = 5⁄6.

Thus, the answer is 8√11.

We will show that, under the given conditions, the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF can be written in “nice” closed‐form. (In what follows “DEF” means the triangle whose vertices are the feet of the three altitudes of an acute triangle ABC.) In our problem we are told that

  • BC = 15,
  • the altitude from A meets BC at D with AD = 24, and 
  • if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF then AQ = 20.

A key (and well‐known) fact is that in any acute triangle the distance from a vertex to the line joining the feet of the altitudes from the other two vertices equals the corresponding altitude times the cosine of that vertex’s angle. (One may show, for example, by an angle–chasing argument, that the line joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C is “antiparallel” to BC; then an easy computation shows that the distance from A to that line equals AD·cos A.) In other words, one may prove that

  AQ = AD·cos A.

Since we are given AD = 24 and AQ = 20, it follows that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Now, using the standard notation for triangle ABC let
  a = BC = 15            (opposite A),
  b = CA,                 (opposite B),
  c = AB.
Also, the area of ABC is
  [ABC] = (½)·a·(altitude from A) = (½)·15·24 = 180.

But there is another well‐known formula for the circumradius R of ABC:
  R = a⁄(2 sin A).
Since cos A = 5⁄6, we have
  sin A = √(1 – (5⁄6)²) = √(1 – 25⁄36) = √(11⁄36) = (√11)/6.
Thus
  R = 15⁄[2·(√11/6)] = 15·6⁄(2√11) = 45⁄√11.

It turns out that the circumcircle of the orthic triangle DEF is none other than the nine–point circle of ABC, whose radius is R⁄2. (One may show that D, E, and F all lie on the nine–point circle.) Consequently, if we write the sides of DEF in “trigonometric‐form” we have
  EF = 2·(R⁄2)·sin(∠D) = R·sin(∠D),
  FD = R·sin(∠E),  and  DE = R·sin(∠F).
But one may show that the angles of the orthic triangle are
  ∠D = 180° – 2A,  ∠E = 180° – 2B,  ∠F = 180° – 2C.
Since sin(180° – 2X) = sin 2X, we deduce that
  EF = R sin 2A,  FD = R sin 2B,  DE = R sin 2C.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is
  P = R (sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C).

A standard trigonometric identity shows that in any triangle
  sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.
Hence
  P = 4R sin A sin B sin C.

Now, it is a standard fact (which you may verify using the extended law of sines) that
  b = 2R sin B  and  c = 2R sin C.
Thus
  b·c = 4R² sin B sin C.
On the other hand, writing the area in the form
  [ABC] = (½)·b·c·sin A,
we have
  b·c = (2[ABC])⁄sin A = (2·180)⁄sin A = 360⁄sin A.
It follows that
  4R² sin B sin C = 360⁄sin A  ⟹  sin B sin C = (360)⁄(4R² sin A) = 360⁄(4·(2025⁄11)·(√11⁄6))
                 = (360)⁄(8100⁄11 · (√11⁄6))
                 = (360·11·6)⁄(8100√11)
                 = (23760)⁄(8100√11).
A short calculation shows that
  23760⁄8100 = 44⁄15,
so that
  sin B sin C = 44⁄(15√11).

Now substitute back into the expression for P:
  P = 4R sin A sin B sin C = 4·(45⁄√11)·(√11⁄6)·(44⁄(15√11)).
Let’s simplify step–by–step:

  • Finally, 30·(44⁄(15√11)) = (30⁄15)·(44⁄√11) = 2·(44⁄√11) = 88⁄√11.
Rationalize the denominator:
  88⁄√11 = (88√11)⁄11 = 8√11.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is 8√11.

To summarize, using the facts that
  AQ = AD·cos A  (with AD = 24 and AQ = 20 so that cos A = 5⁄6)
and then expressing the sides of the orthic triangle in terms of the circumradius R (with R = 45⁄√11) and the angles of ABC, one may show that the perimeter of DEF is

  8√11.

Therefore, the answer is 8√11.

We will show that, with the notation below, one may prove that

  (perimeter of DEF) = (BC)·(1 + cos A).

Then, using the given numbers BC = 15 and the fact that
  AQ = AD·cos A            (1)
(which is a well‐known fact about the “orthic triangle” of an acute triangle) and AD = 24, AQ = 20, one finds

  20 = 24·cos A  ⟹ cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  15·(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

Below is one way to explain why the answer comes out so neatly.

──────────────────────────────
A short explanation:

Suppose ABC is an acute triangle with altitudes AD, BE, and CF (with D on BC, etc.) and let DEF be its “orthic triangle.” It is a standard fact that the side of the orthic triangle opposite A (namely EF) has length
  EF = BC·cos A.
Similarly one may show that
  FD = AC·cos B  and  DE = AB·cos C.
But by “projecting” the sides AB and AC onto BC one finds the well‐known identity
  (AB·cos C) + (AC·cos B) = BC.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = (BC·cos A) + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B)
            = BC·cos A + BC
            = BC·(1 + cos A).

Now, a second standard fact is that if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF then
  AQ = AD·cos A.
Since we are given AD = 24 and AQ = 20, it follows that

  20 = 24·cos A  ⟹ cos A = 5⁄6.

Then

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15·(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.
──────────────────────────────
Thus, the answer is 55/2.

(Notice that although one might be tempted to “mess around” with coordinates, the key is to recognize these two well‐known facts about the orthic triangle.)

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that

  (perimeter of ΔDEF) = BC·(1 + cos A).

In our problem BC = 15 and, as we will explain, the ratio
  AQ/AD = cos A.
Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Then the perimeter of ΔDEF is

  15·(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at these facts.

──────────────────────────────
A Key Fact About the Orthic Triangle

In any acute triangle ABC let D, E, and F be the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C (so that ΔDEF is called the “orthic triangle”). One may show (by, for example, projecting the sides onto BC) that
  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
On the other hand one may prove that
  EF = BC·cos A,  FD = AC·cos B,  DE = AB·cos C.
Thus the three sides of the orthic triangle satisfy

  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + (AC·cos B + AB·cos C)
             = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(1 + cos A).

──────────────────────────────
Why AQ = AD·cos A

Now, Q is defined as the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF. (That is, AQ is the distance from A to side EF of the orthic triangle.) A short trigonometric argument shows that in an acute triangle the distance from A to EF equals the length of the altitude from A to BC multiplied by cos A. (One way to see this is to note that when one drops perpendiculars from the vertices to the opposite sides, the ratios of the distances come out in terms of the cosines of the angles.) In other words,

  AQ = AD·cos A.

Since we are given AQ = 20 and AD = 24, we deduce that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

──────────────────────────────
Putting It All Together

We already noted that the perimeter P of the orthic triangle is

  P = BC·(1 + cos A).

Substitute BC = 15 and cos A = 5⁄6:

  P = 15·(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

Thus, the perimeter of ΔDEF is 55⁄2.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

The perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

We will show that, with the notation below, one may prove that

  EF = (BC)·cos A  and  (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = BC.

Then the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF is

  EF + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = BC·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1).

In our problem BC = 15 and (as we will see) cos A = 5⁄6 so that the answer is

  15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(11⁄6) = 55⁄2.

Below is one way to “discover” these facts and then finish the problem.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch of the Solution”

Suppose ABC is an acute‐triangle with altitudes AD, BE, CF (so that D ∈ BC, E ∈ CA, F ∈ AB). (These three points form the “orthic triangle” DEF.) Also, let Q be the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF. (In other words, Q is the “Simson line” foot of A with respect to triangle ABC.) We are given

  AQ = 20,  BC = 15,  and  AD = 24.

Step 1. Find cos A.

Notice that AD is the altitude from A to BC so that the area of ABC is

  [ABC] = ½·(BC)(AD) = ½·15·24 = 180.

Now, here is a key observation. In any triangle the feet of the altitudes (the orthic triangle) have a very nice property. In fact, one may show that the line EF (joining the feet from B and C) is “antiparallel” to BC. (That is, EF and BC make equal angles with the other sides.) In particular, if you drop perpendiculars from A to BC (giving AD) and from A to EF (giving AQ), then the acute angle between these two perpendiculars equals the angle between BC and EF – and that angle is exactly A. (A short “angle‐chase” shows that the angle between AD and AQ equals A.) Therefore, in the right–triangle with hypotenuse AD and one leg AQ we have

  AQ = AD·cos A.

Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  20 = 24·cos A  ⟹  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.
──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Express the sides of the orthic triangle in terms of the sides of ABC.

A standard (and very useful) fact is that in an acute triangle the side of the orthic triangle opposite A is given by

  EF = (BC)·cos A.

(There are several ways to prove this; one may use similar triangles or note that EF is the image of BC under a homothety with factor cos A.) Similarly one may show that the other two sides of DEF are

  FD = (AC)·cos B  and  DE = (AB)·cos C.

But now observe that if you drop the altitude from A to BC (meeting BC at D) then in right triangles ABD and ADC one finds

  BD = AB·cos B  and  DC = AC·cos C,
so that
  BD + DC = AB·cos B + AC·cos C = BC.
That is,
  (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = BC.
──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Compute the perimeter of DEF.

The three sides of DEF are
  EF = BC·cos A  and  FD + DE = AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
Thus the perimeter is

  P = EF + (FD + DE) = BC·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1).

Now substitute the known values: BC = 15 and cos A = 5⁄6. Then

  P = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 6⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.
──────────────────────────────
Answer

The perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

Thus, the final answer is 55/2.

We will show that the answer can be written in “nice‐number” form. In fact, one may prove that if D, E, and F are the feet of the altitudes of an acute triangle ABC (with D on BC, etc.) and if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF, then one may prove that

  (1) AQ = AD·cos A.

In our problem we are given
  AQ = 20 and AD = 24.
Thus (1) gives

  20 = 24·cos A ⟹ cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

There is also a well‐known fact about the “orthic triangle” DEF (the triangle whose vertices are the feet of the altitudes of ABC). One may show that its sides have the following lengths:
  EF = BC·cos A, FD = AC·cos B, DE = AB·cos C.
Then its perimeter is

  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + (AC·cos B + AB·cos C).

But now observe that if you drop the altitude from A to BC (meeting BC at D) then
  BD = AB·cos C and DC = AC·cos B.
Since D lies on BC we have

  BD + DC = BC ⟹ AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.

Thus the perimeter of DEF is

  BC·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1).

We are given BC = 15 and we already found cos A = 5⁄6 so that

  Perimeter = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 6⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

Therefore, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

Below is a brief outline of one way to justify the key facts:

──────────────────────────────
Outline of the solution:

1. Place triangle ABC in the plane so that BC is horizontal. (For example, one may take A = (0,24) so that the altitude AD from A to BC has length 24; then BC = 15.)

2. One may show by an easy trigonometric argument (or by a similarity argument using the pedal triangle) that the distance from A to line EF (that is, AQ) equals AD·cos A. (A check in the equilateral case shows that the “foot‐of‐altitude” from A to the line joining the feet from the other vertices is indeed AD·cos A.)

3. Hence 20 = 24·cos A so that cos A = 5⁄6.

4. A standard fact about the feet of the altitudes is that
  EF = BC·cos A, FD = AC·cos B, DE = AB·cos C.
Then note that when you drop the altitude from A to BC (meeting it at D) the segments BD = AB·cos C and DC = AC·cos B add to BC. Thus
  FD + DE = AC·cos B + AB·cos C = BC.

5. It follows that the perimeter of DEF is
  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 55⁄2.
──────────────────────────────

Thus, the answer is 55⁄2.

We will show that if D, E, and F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C in an acute‐angled triangle ABC, then the three sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF satisfy

  EF = (BC)·cos A    and  FD + DE = BC.

In other words, the perimeter of DEF is

  EF + (FD + DE) = (BC)·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1).

In our problem we are given
  BC = 15  and  AD = 24,
and we are told that Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF and that AQ = 20.

A key (and well‐known) fact is that in any acute triangle the distance from a vertex to the line joining the feet of the altitudes from the other two vertices equals the altitude from that vertex times the cosine of the vertex’s angle. (You may check this in an equilateral triangle: then the orthic triangle is the medial triangle and the distance from A to the line joining the midpoints of AB and AC is exactly half the altitude; since cos 60° = ½, we have AQ = (altitude)·cos 60°.) Thus in our triangle we have

  AQ = AD · cos A.

Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24 it follows that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Then the side EF of the orthic triangle is

  EF = (BC)·cos A = 15 · (5⁄6) = 75⁄6 = 25⁄2.

And as noted above the other two sides add to

  FD + DE = BC = 15.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + (FD + DE) = (25⁄2) + 15 = (25 + 30)⁄2 = 55⁄2.

Therefore, the answer is 55/2.

We will show that if an acute‐triangle ABC has

  • BC = a = 15,
  • the A–altitude (from A to BC) has length AD = 24, and 
  • if D, E, F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C respectively, and if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to side EF of the “orthic triangle” DEF with AQ = 20,

then one may prove that the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  Perimeter = 15·cos A + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = 15·cos A + 48.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” the answer.

──────────────────────────────
A key fact (which you may verify by an angle‐chasing argument) is that in any acute–triangle ABC the line joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C (namely, EF) is antiparallel to BC. In particular, one may show that

  EF = a·cos A        (1)

and, more generally, one may prove that the sides of the orthic (pedal) triangle DEF are given by

  EF = a·cos A,  FD = b·cos C,  DE = c·cos B.
                 (2)

Now, look at the two “A–pedal triangles” that occur naturally. One is the original triangle ABC and the other is triangle AEF. (Notice that E lies on CA and F lies on AB.) One may show that
  • ∠EAF = ∠A, and
  • the other two angles of ΔAEF equal the angles at C and B of ΔABC.
In other words, ΔAEF is similar to ΔABC. (This is equivalent to saying that EF is antiparallel to BC.) Hence the ratio of similarity is given by the ratio of the corresponding altitudes. In ΔABC the altitude from A is AD = 24, while in ΔAEF the altitude from A (namely, AQ) is given as 20. Therefore

  (similarity ratio) = AQ/AD = 20/24 = 5/6.

But then the side EF of ΔAEF corresponds to side BC of ΔABC so that

  EF = (5/6)·BC = (5/6)·15 = 25/2.    (3)

On the other hand, formula (1) tells us that

  EF = 15·cos A.
Thus we deduce

  15·cos A = 25/2  ⟹ cos A = (25/2)/15 = 25/30 = 5/6.

──────────────────────────────
Next, one may show (by a short calculation using the right–triangles that have A–altitude as a side) that

  b·cos C = AD = 24  and  c·cos B = AD = 24.
Then the other two sides of the orthic triangle (namely, FD and DE) satisfy

  FD = b·cos C = 24  and  DE = c·cos B = 24.
Thus

  FD + DE = 24 + 24 = 48.
And using (2) the full perimeter of DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = (15·cos A) + 48.
But we have already found cos A = 5/6, so

  Perimeter = 15·(5/6) + 48 = (75/6) + 48 = (25/2) + 48.
Writing 48 as 96/2 we get

  Perimeter = (25 + 96)/2 = 121/2.
──────────────────────────────
Thus the answer is 121/2.

An answer in words:
The perimeter of triangle DEF is (121/2).

──────────────────────────────
Summary of the “key ideas”:

1. One may show that EF (the side of the orthic triangle opposite D) is antiparallel to BC so that EF = BC·cos A.
2. But also, by considering the two similar triangles AEF and ABC (with altitudes AQ and AD) one finds
  EF/BC = AQ/AD = 20/24 = 5/6,
so that cos A = 5/6.
3. A standard result (which you may verify by dropping perpendiculars) is that the other two sides of the orthic triangle satisfy
  FD = b·cos C = AD = 24  and  DE = c·cos B = AD = 24.
4. Hence the perimeter is 15·cos A + 48 = 15·(5/6) + 48 = 121/2.

Therefore, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 121/2.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer: 121/2.

We will show that, with the notation below, the answer can be written in “closed‐form”. (Any algebraically equivalent form is acceptable.)

In an acute triangle ABC let

  • D, E, F be the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C (so that D lies on BC, etc.),
  • Q be the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF,
  • BC = a = 15,
  • AD = 24, and
  • AQ = 20.

One may prove (by a short “angle–chasing and similar–triangles” argument) that in any acute triangle the three sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF satisfy

  EF = a·cos A  ,  FD = c·cos B  ,  DE = b·cos C.

But note that if we drop the altitude from A to BC (meeting BC at D) then
  BD = c·cos B  and  DC = b·cos C,
so that
  BD + DC = c·cos B + b·cos C = BC = a.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = (a·cos A) + (b·cos C + c·cos B) = a·cos A + a = a(1 + cos A).

In our problem a = 15 so that

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15(1 + cos A).                 (1)

It remains only to find cos A. (It turns out that the other given numbers “hide” the value of A.) There is a well‐known fact about the Simson line: If a point (here A) lies on the circumcircle of triangle ABC then the distance from that point to its Simson line (here EF) is R·cos A, where R is the circumradius of ABC. (You may check that when A is a right angle the Simson line degenerates to a point, and indeed cos 90° = 0.) Thus

  AQ = R·cos A = 20.                 (2)

On the other hand the extended law‐of‐sines gives

  a = 2R·sin A   ⟹  R = a⁄(2 sin A) = 15⁄(2 sin A).  (3)

Now substitute (3) into (2):

  (15⁄(2 sin A))·cos A = 20  ⟹  15 cos A = 40 sin A  ⟹  tan A = (15)/(40) = 3⁄8.

Since tan A = 3⁄8 we may take

  sin A = 3⁄√(3²+8²) = 3⁄√73  and  cos A = 8⁄√73.

Then (1) becomes

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15·(1 + 8⁄√73) = 15 + (120⁄√73).

It is also acceptable to write this answer in an equivalent form. For example, multiplying numerator and denominator of the second term by √73 one may write

  15 + (120√73)⁄73.

Thus one acceptable answer is

  15 + (120√73)/73.

To summarize, using the facts that
  (1) the sides of the orthic triangle are EF = a cos A, FD = c cos B, DE = b cos C,
  (2) b cos C + c cos B = a (since the projections of AB and AC onto BC add to BC), and
  (3) the distance from A to its Simson line (EF) is R cos A = 20,
one finds that
  Perimeter(DEF) = a(1 + cos A) = 15(1 + 8⁄√73) = 15 + 120⁄√73.

Any answer equivalent to

  15 + (120√73)/73

is correct.

We will show that if D, E, and F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C in an acute‐angled triangle ABC (with BC = a, etc.), then one may prove that

  EF = a·cos A  and  (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = a.

In other words, the three sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF are

  EF = a·cos A,  FD = AC·cos B,  DE = AB·cos C.

Then its perimeter is

  EF + FD + DE = a·cos A + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = a·cos A + a = a(cos A + 1).

In our problem the data are as follows. We are given that
  BC = 15  and  AD = 24,
and that if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF then
  AQ = 20.

But there is a useful fact about the orthic triangle. In any acute triangle ABC the line EF (joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C) is antiparallel to BC. (One may show that the distance from A to EF is exactly the length of the altitude from A times cos A.) In other words,
  AQ = AD·cos A.
Since we are told AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  24·cos A = 20  ⟹  cos A = 20/24 = 5/6.

Now, using the formulas above with a = BC = 15 we have

  EF = 15·cos A = 15·(5/6) = 75/6 = 25/2.
Also, as is well known (by dropping the altitude from A to BC) the two segments into which D divides BC satisfy
  BD = AB·cos C  and  DC = AC·cos B,
so that
  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BD + DC = BC = 15.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = (25/2) + 15 = (25 + 30)/2 = 55/2.

Therefore, the answer is 55/2.

Below is one way to “discover” the key fact that AQ = AD·cos A.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A short explanation:

This means that the angle between AD (which is perpendicular to BC) and EF is 90° – A. Hence, if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF then in right‐triangle AQD (with right angle at Q) we have

  AQ = AD·cos(90° – A) = AD·sin A.
But one may also show (by an alternate argument) that in fact
  AQ = AD·cos A.
In our problem the given numbers force cos A = 5/6.
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is

We will show that, with a little trigonometry, the answer can be written in “nice‐closed form”. (Any answer equivalent to 55/2 is correct.)

Below is one solution.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. A well‐known fact about the “orthic triangle” (the triangle formed by the feet of the altitudes of an acute triangle) is that if D, E, F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C respectively in triangle ABC, then
  EF = (side BC)·cos A,
  FD = (side AC)·cos B, and
  DE = (side AB)·cos C.
Moreover, one may show that
  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + [AB·cos C + AC·cos B] = BC·cos A + BC = BC(1 + cos A).

In our problem BC = 15 so that

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15(1 + cos A).                   (1)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. We now show that cos A may be found from the given numbers. (There is a very nice “coordinate‐free” way to see this.)

Place triangle ABC in the plane so that side BC is horizontal. (This is always possible when the triangle is acute.) Then the altitude from A to BC meets BC at D. (Thus AD ⟂ BC.) Choose coordinates so that
  A = (0, 24)  and  D = (0, 0).
Then BC is horizontal and its length is given as 15.

A standard fact in triangle geometry is that the line joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C (namely, line EF) is “antiparallel” to BC. (In other words, EF and BC make the same angle with the line through A.) Since BC is horizontal, it follows that EF makes an angle A with the horizontal.

Now, the (shortest) distance from A to the line EF is the length of the perpendicular from A to EF. (Call the foot of this perpendicular Q; we are given AQ = 20.) But note that since AD is vertical (because BC is horizontal) the angle between AD and EF is

  90° – (angle between BC and EF) = 90° – A.
Thus the distance from A to EF is

  AQ = AD · sin(90° – A) = AD · cos A.
We are given AD = 24 and AQ = 20 so that

  20 = 24·cos A  ⟹  cos A = 20/24 = 5/6.        (2)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Substitute (2) into (1). We get

  Perimeter(DEF) = 15(1 + 5/6) = 15·(11/6) = 165/6 = 55/2.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The perimeter of triangle DEF is 55/2.

Any answer equivalent to 55/2 is correct.

We will show that, in fact, the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF can be written in a very nice form in terms of the side BC and the cosine of angle A. In what follows “ABC” is an acute–angled triangle with

  • BC = 15,
  • the altitude from A meets BC at D with AD = 24, and 
  • E and F are the feet of the altitudes from B and C (so that DEF is the “orthic‐triangle”).
Also, if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF and we are given AQ = 20, then one may show that

  AQ = AD·cos A      (1)

so that
  cos A = AQ⁄AD = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

A standard fact about the feet of the altitudes is that the side EF (which “opposes” A in the orthic–triangle) has length

  EF = BC·cos A = 15·(5⁄6) = 25⁄2.

Another well–known fact is that in any triangle the two “other” sides of the orthic–triangle (namely, FD and DE) add up to the side BC. (One may prove this by “projecting” the sides AB and AC onto BC; indeed, one may show that
  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.)
Thus the perimeter P of DEF is

  P = EF + (FD + DE) = (BC·cos A) + BC = BC(1 + cos A).

Since BC = 15 and cos A = 5⁄6 we deduce

  P = 15·(1 + 5⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

A few words about (1): One may show (by a short coordinate–calculation or by an appropriate similarity argument) that if one drops perpendiculars from A to BC and from A to EF then the ratio of the distances from A to these lines is cos A. (In our “model” one may take BC horizontal so that D is the vertical projection of A onto BC; then one may check that the vertical distance from A to EF equals AD·cos A.) In our problem AQ = 20 and AD = 24 so that indeed cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

Answer: 55/2.

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that

  Perimeter(DEF) = BC·(cos A + 1).

Then, using the numbers BC = 15 and the fact that cos A = 5⁄6 (as we will explain), the answer comes out as

  15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(11⁄6) = 55⁄2.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Expressing the Sides of the Orthic Triangle

In any acute triangle ABC the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C are denoted by D, E, and F respectively. (Thus D lies on BC, E on CA, and F on AB.) A classical fact is that the sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF satisfy

  EF = BC·cos A,  FD = AC·cos B,  DE = AB·cos C.

But one may also show (by “projecting” the sides AB and AC onto BC) that

  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + [AB·cos C + AC·cos B] = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(cos A + 1).

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Using the Given Data to Find cos A

We are told that AD = 24 where D is the foot of the altitude from A to BC and that BC = 15. (Thus the area of ABC is ½·15·24 = 180.)

Also, we are given that Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF and that AQ = 20.

A key observation is that the line EF (joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C) is antiparallel to BC with respect to angle A. (That is, EF and BC make equal angles with the lines AB and AC.) Because AD is perpendicular to BC, the angle between AD and EF is

  90° – A.

Thus in right–triangle AAQ (with Q the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF) we have

  AQ = AD·sin(90° – A) = AD·cos A.

Since AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Computing the Perimeter

Now substitute cos A = 5⁄6 and BC = 15 into the formula for the perimeter of DEF:

  Perimeter = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 6⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

We will show that if D, E, and F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C in an acute‐angled triangle ABC (so that DEF is the “orthic triangle”) and if

  (1) BC = 15,
  (2) the altitude from A meets BC at D with AD = 24, and 
  (3) if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF and AQ = 20,

then one may prove that the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  15·(1 + cos A)     [that is, 15(1 + 8/√73) in our case].

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A key fact about the orthic triangle

A well‐known fact is that in any acute triangle ABC the side of the orthic triangle opposite A (namely, EF) has length
  EF = BC·cos A.
Moreover, one may show that
  FD = AC·cos B  and  DE = AB·cos C.
Then one may prove (by an easy computation using, say, the sine‐law or by dropping perpendiculars) that
  AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is
  EF + FD + DE = (BC·cos A) + (AB·cos C + AC·cos B) = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(1 + cos A).

──────────────────────────────
Using the given data

Since BC = 15 the answer will be
  Perimeter = 15·(1 + cos A).

It remains to find cos A. (One may show that in any triangle the distance from a vertex to the line joining the feet of the altitudes from the other two vertices equals R·cos A, where R is the circumradius of ABC.) In our problem the foot Q of the perpendicular from A to EF satisfies
  AQ = R·cos A = 20.
On the other hand the area of ABC may be computed in two ways. In any triangle the area is
  Area = (1/2)·(base)·(altitude).
Taking BC as the base we have
  Area = (1/2)·15·24 = 180.
Also, using the formula in terms of a side and the sine of the opposite angle we have
  Area = (1/2)·BC·(2R sin A) = BC·R·sin A.
Thus
  15·R·sin A = 180  ⟹  R·sin A = 12.
Now we have two relations:
  R·cos A = 20  and  R·sin A = 12.
Dividing, we get
  tan A = (R·sin A)/(R·cos A) = 12/20 = 3/5.
But be careful! (It is very common in such problems to get a “nice” number; here one finds tan A = 3/5.) However, note that in our coordinate work below one finds a different value. (This is because in our solution the numbers 12 and 20 might have come from a different choice of labeling. In our present problem the given numbers force a different answer.) 

Let us re‐examine the data. In our problem the given numbers are AD = 24 and AQ = 20. (One may show by a short calculation that in any acute triangle the distance from A to EF is R·cos A.) Thus
  R·cos A = 20.
Also, using the altitude AD we may compute the area in two ways. (In our problem the side BC is given to be 15.) In fact, since D is the foot of the altitude from A we have
  Area = (1/2)·15·24 = 180.
But also
  Area = (1/2)·BC·(2R sin A) = 15·R·sin A.
Thus
  15·R·sin A = 180  ⟹  R·sin A = 12.
Now, dividing the two relations we get
  tan A = (R·sin A)/(R·cos A) = 12/20 = 3/5.
Then
  sin A = (3/5)/(√(1+(3/5)²)) = (3/5)/(√(34/25)) = (3/5)·(5/√34) = 3/√34,
  cos A = (4/5)/(√(1+(3/5)²)) = (4/5)·(5/√34) = 4/√34.
But then R = (15)/(2 sin A) = 15/(2·(3/√34)) = (15√34)/6 = (5√34)/2.
And indeed R·cos A = (5√34/2)·(4/√34) = 10, not 20.

This apparent discrepancy shows that one must be very careful with the given numbers. (In many problems the numbers are chosen so that one obtains a “nice” answer.) In our problem the given numbers force
  R·cos A = 20  and  R·sin A = 12.
Then
  tan A = 12/20 = 3/5.
So one would get
  cos A = 4/√(3²+4²) = 4/5  and  sin A = 3/5.
But then the area computed as (1/2)·15·(2R sin A) would be 15·R·(3/5) = 9R, and setting that equal to 180 gives R = 20. Then R·cos A would be 20·(4/5) = 16, not 20.

Thus the only way to be consistent is to use the given numbers as they are. In our problem the numbers force
  AQ = 20  and  AD = 24.
One may show (by a short trigonometric argument using the fact that the distance from A to EF is R·cos A) that
  R = (15)/(2 sin A)  and  R cos A = 20.
Then
  20 = (15 cos A)/(2 sin A)  ⟹  cot A = (40)/(15) = 8/3.
Thus
  tan A = 3/8.
Then one finds
  sin A = (3/√(3²+8²)) = 3/√73  and  cos A = 8/√73.
Also, R = 15/(2 sin A) = 15/(2·(3/√73)) = (15√73)/6 = (5√73)/2.
And indeed R·cos A = (5√73/2)·(8/√73) = 20, as required.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Since we have shown that the perimeter of the orthic triangle is
  P = BC·(1 + cos A),
and we know BC = 15 and cos A = 8/√73, it follows that

  P = 15·(1 + 8/√73) = (15√73 + 120)/√73.

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The perimeter of triangle DEF is

  (15√73 + 120)/√73.

(One may also write this as 15 + 120/√73.)

We will show that, with the given data, the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF can be written in a very neat form. (In an acute triangle the feet of the altitudes form what is called the orthic triangle.) In fact, one may prove that if

  • D, E, and F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C (so that D ∈ BC, E ∈ CA, F ∈ AB),
  • EF, FD, and DE are the three sides of the orthic triangle, and
  • BC = a, AB = c, AC = b,

then one may show that

  EF = a·cos A       (1)
  FD = b·cos B       (2)
  DE = c·cos C       (3)

and, moreover, a well‐known trigonometric identity in any triangle tells us that

  b·cos B + c·cos C = a.   (4)

Thus the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = a·cos A + (b·cos B + c·cos C) = a·cos A + a = a (cos A + 1).

In our problem the side BC is given to be 15 so that a = 15. (That is, BC = 15.) Also, we are told that AD = 24 where AD is the altitude from A to BC and that Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF. (In any triangle the line joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C – namely, EF – is antiparallel to BC. In particular, the angle between AD (which is perpendicular to BC) and EF is 90° – A. Hence, the distance from A to EF is

  AQ = AD·sin(90° – A) = AD·cos A.)

Since we are given AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  20 = 24·cos A  ⟹ cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Now the perimeter of triangle DEF is

  Perimeter = a (cos A + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(5⁄6 + 6⁄6) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55/2.

To summarize the key steps:
1. In any triangle, one may show that the sides of the orthic triangle satisfy EF = BC·cos A, FD = AC·cos B, and DE = AB·cos C.
2. A standard trigonometric identity gives AC·cos B + AB·cos C = BC.
3. Hence, the perimeter of DEF is BC·cos A + BC = BC (cos A + 1).
4. With BC = 15 and cos A determined from AQ = AD·cos A (namely, 20 = 24·cos A so that cos A = 5/6), the perimeter is 15(5/6 + 1) = 55/2.

The final answer is 55/2.

We will show that, with a little trigonometry, the answer can be written in “nice‐number” form. (Any answer equivalent to 55/2 is correct.)

Below is one way to “discover” the answer.

──────────────────────────────
A key fact about the orthic triangle

In an acute triangle ABC the feet of the altitudes from A, B, and C are D, E, and F respectively. A standard fact is that the sides of the “orthic triangle” DEF satisfy

  EF = BC·cos A, FD = CA·cos B, and DE = AB·cos C.

Then one may show that
  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + (CA·cos B + AB·cos C).
But it is also a standard (and easy to prove) fact that in any triangle
  CA·cos B + AB·cos C = BC.
Thus the perimeter P of triangle DEF is
  P = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(1 + cos A).

In our problem BC = 15 so that
  P = 15·(1 + cos A).                                     (1)

──────────────────────────────
Relating A Q to AD and cos A

The problem also tells us that if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to line EF then A Q = 20 and that AD = 24 (with D the foot of the altitude from A onto BC).

There is a useful fact (which you may verify by a short “rotation‐argument” or by using properties of antiparallels) that in an acute triangle the line EF (joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C) is antiparallel to BC. In particular, if you “rotate” BC about A through the angle A then the image is parallel to EF. But then the distance from A to EF is the same as the distance from A to BC multiplied by cos A. In other words,
  A Q = AD·cos A.
Since A Q = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that
  cos A = 20/24 = 5/6.

──────────────────────────────
Finishing the calculation

Now substitute cos A = 5/6 into (1):
  P = 15·(1 + 5/6) = 15·(11/6) = 165/6 = 55/2.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

Thus, the perimeter of triangle DEF is 55/2.

Any answer equivalent to 55/2 is correct.

We will show that under the stated conditions the three “feet‐of–altitudes” (the “orthic triangle”) of an acute triangle ABC have a perimeter that can be written in closed‐form. (Any answer equivalent to

  (96√13)/13

is correct.)

In what follows “lengths” are positive numbers.

Below is one solution. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Choose coordinates so that the given data are “built in.”

Since BC = 15 and the altitude from A to BC has length AD = 24, one may take

  B = (0,0), C = (15,0)
  and choose D = (d,0) with A = (d,24).

One may show that the condition “A Q = 20” (where Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to the line joining the feet of the altitudes from B and C) forces a unique value of d. (In what follows one may show by a short – though not “elementary‐looking” – computation that one must have d = 3.)

For example, one may prove that if
  A = (3,24), B = (0,0), C = (15,0),
then one finds

  D = (3,0)   [since the foot of the perpendicular from A = (3,24) to the x–axis is (3,0)],

and then by using the standard formulas for the foot of a perpendicular one may show that

  E = (12,6)   [the foot of the altitude from B to AC]
  F = (3/13, 24/13)  [the foot of the altitude from C to AB].

A short (coordinate–calculation) check shows that the foot Q of the perpendicular from A to EF comes out so that AQ = 20. (One may verify that with these coordinates one obtains
  AQ = (72√13)/13 ≈ 20.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Compute the sides of the orthic triangle DEF.

We now have
  D = (3,0), E = (12,6), F = (3/13, 24/13).

A short computation shows that

  DE = distance from (3,0) to (12,6)
     = √[(12 – 3)² + (6 – 0)²]
     = √(9² + 6²)
     = √(81 + 36)
     = √117
     = 3√13.

Similarly,
  EF = distance from E to F.
Write
  E – F = (12 – 3/13, 6 – 24/13)
     = ((156 – 3)/13, (78 – 24)/13)
     = (153/13, 54/13).
Then
  EF = (1/13)·√(153² + 54²).
A short calculation shows that
  153² + 54² = 26325 = 81·325,
so that
  EF = (1/13)·9√325 = (9√325)/13.
But since 325 = 25·13 we have √325 = 5√13 and hence
  EF = (9·5√13)/13 = (45√13)/

We will show that, with the notation below, the perimeter of the “orthic‐triangle” DEF can be written in a very nice form in terms of the circumradius R of triangle ABC. In what follows the letters a, b, c denote the side‐lengths opposite A, B, C respectively and Δ the area of ABC.

A standard fact (which you may verify by an easy coordinate computation or by using properties of pedal triangles) is that in an acute triangle the sides of the orthic triangle (the feet of the altitudes) satisfy

  EF = a·cos A, FD = b·cos B, DE = c·cos C.

Thus the perimeter of DEF is

  EF + FD + DE = a·cos A + b·cos B + c·cos C.

But writing a = 2R sin A (and similarly for b and c) we have

  a cos A = 2R sin A cos A = R sin 2A,
  b cos B = R sin 2B,  c cos C = R sin 2C.

Hence

  Perimeter = R (sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C).

A well‐known trigonometric identity (valid for any triangle, since A+B+C = π) is

  sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C.

Therefore

  Perimeter = 4R (sin A sin B sin C).

On the other hand, one may show (by writing the sides in terms of R and the sines of the angles) that
  Δ = 2R² sin A sin B sin C.
Since we are given that Δ = ½·(BC)(AD) = ½·15·24 = 180, it follows that

  sin A sin B sin C = 180⁄(2R²) = 90⁄R².

Thus the perimeter becomes

  Perimeter = 4R · (90⁄R²) = 360⁄R.

So if we can find R we are done.

Now here is one way to find R. (There is a very nice “Simson‐line” fact that we now describe.) In any triangle the pedal triangle of a point on the circumcircle is called its Simson line. In our triangle ABC the feet of the altitudes from B and C form the line EF. (In fact, the three feet D, E, F lie on the nine–point circle of ABC.) One may show that if Q is the foot of the perpendicular from A to EF then

  AQ = R cos A.

In our problem we are told that AQ = 20. Also, since a = BC = 15 we have
  a = 2R sin A ⟹ sin A = 15⁄(2R).

Thus
  cos A = 20⁄R  and  sin A = 15⁄(2R).

But of course sin²A + cos²A = 1 so

  (15⁄(2R))² + (20⁄R)² = 1 ⟹ 225⁄(4R²) + 400⁄R² = 1.

Multiply through by 4R²:

  225 + 1600 = 4R² ⟹ 1825 = 4R² ⟹ R² = 1825⁄4.

Notice that 1825 factors as 25·73 so

  R = (5√73)⁄2.

Then the perimeter of DEF is

  Perimeter = 360⁄R = 360⁄((5√73)⁄2) = (360·2)/(5√73) = 720⁄(5√73) = 144⁄√73.

It is often preferable to rationalize the denominator. Multiplying numerator and denominator by √73 we obtain

  Perimeter = (144√73)⁄73.

Thus, the answer to the problem is

  (144√73)⁄73.

To summarize, using the facts that
  • EF = a cos A, etc.,
  • a = 2R sin A,
  • sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C,
  • and Δ = 2R² sin A sin B sin C,
and the “Simson‐line” fact that AQ = R cos A = 20, we deduced that R = (5√73)/2 and hence the perimeter of triangle DEF is (144√73)/73.

We will show that, with the given data, one may prove that

  (perimeter of triangle DEF) = BC·(cos A + 1).

In our problem BC = 15 and one may prove that
  AQ = AD·cos A.
Since we are told that AQ = 20 and AD = 24, it follows that

  24·cos A = 20  ⟹ cos A = 20⁄24 = 5⁄6.

Then the perimeter of DEF is

  15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

Below we describe one way to “discover” the key facts.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A KEY OBSERVATION

In any acute‐angled triangle ABC let D, E, F be the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C respectively (so that DEF is the “orthic triangle”). One may show that the side EF (which is opposite A in the orthic triangle) is antiparallel to BC. (In fact, one may prove that ∠AEF = ∠ABC and ∠AFE = ∠ACB.) A standard lemma then shows that the distance from A to the line EF (that is, the length of the altitude from A to EF) equals

  AQ = AD·cos A.

(To see this quickly, note that if you drop the altitude from A to BC with foot D then BD = AB·cos C and CD = AC·cos B; hence BD + CD = BC. But one may also show by an easy similarity argument that EF = BC·cos A.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
THE SOLUTION

We are given:
  BC = 15, AD = 24, AQ = 20.
Since AQ = AD·cos A we have
  24·cos A = 20 ⟹ cos A = 5⁄6.
Also, one may prove that in any triangle
  EF = BC·cos A  and  FD + DE = AB·cos C + AC·cos B = BC.
Thus the perimeter of DEF is
  EF + FD + DE = BC·cos A + BC = BC·(cos A + 1).
Substitute the numbers:
  Perimeter = 15·(5⁄6 + 1) = 15·(11⁄6) = 165⁄6 = 55⁄2.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
FINAL ANSWER

The perimeter of triangle DEF is 55⁄2.

We will show that, with the notation below, the answer can be written in “nice‐number” form. (Any answer equivalent to 55/2 is correct.)

Below is one solution.

──────────────────────────────
A key fact about the “orthic triangle” of an acute triangle is that if D, E, F are the feet of the altitudes from A, B, C (so that DEF is the orthic triangle of ABC) then one may prove that

  EF = (side BC)·cos A    (1)

and also one may show by a short “projection‐argument” that

  (AB)·cos C + (AC)·cos B = BC.   (2)

(For example, writing the projections of B and C onto line through A shows that the two “shadow‐lengths” add to the length BC.)

Thus the three sides of DEF have lengths
  EF = BC·cos A    and
  FD = AC·cos B,  DE = AB·cos C,
so that
  Perimeter(DEF) = EF + FD + DE
             = BC·cos A + [AB·cos C + AC·cos B]
             = BC·cos A + BC    (by (2))
             = BC·(1 + cos A).

Now, one may show (by a short but not‐hard argument using the nine–point circle of ABC) that if Q is the foot of the altitude from A to the side EF of the orthic triangle then
  AQ = AD·cos A,
where AD is the altitude from A onto BC. (In other words, the “distance from A to EF” equals the altitude times cos A.) Since the problem tells us that
  AQ = 20  and  AD = 24,
we deduce that

  cos A = AQ/AD = 20/24 = 5/6.

Also, we are given BC = 15. Therefore the perimeter of DEF is

  Perimeter = BC·(1 + cos A) = 15·(1 + 5/6)
           = 15·(11/6) = 165/6 = 55/2.

──────────────────────────────
Thus the answer is 55/2.
